prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, whose magic-wavelength trapping and 10^-18 precision opened new tests of fundamental physics and a new basis for the measurement of time

statement.case_for: I opened with the Higgs experiments at first place and optical lattice clocks third, and I have moved the clocks to the top after reading the other seven ballots. Discoveries come first, and then the people. On the discovery, optical lattice clocks were ranked by seven of eight members, first by two and in the top three by three. The support comes from atomic physics, quantum optics, a statistical-physics member and a particle-physics member alike, so it does not depend on one subfield. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removed the trapping-light shift, and the lattice clocks, driven by Ye's JILA group, now reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. The relativistic redshift is resolved across millimetres, there are searches for variation of constants and for dark-matter signals, and a redefinition of the second is being prepared. This is a clue from nature obtained by measurement, which is the kind of evidence I value over elegant theory that remains unconfirmed. The attribution is the cleanest on the whole shortlist: every ballot that proposed laureates for B002 named the same two people, and the credited set is already of the right size. The work is mature and has been reproduced and surpassed across JILA, RIKEN, NIST, PTB and SYRTE for over a decade, and the 2005 prize (frequency comb) and the 2012 prize (ion control) honoured distinct steps in the lineage.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is the one Eriksson-adjacent and Mehlig-style readers would raise, namely that clocks are an evolution of earlier clock-related prizes (Ramsey, Dehmelt and Paul, Hall and Hansch, Wineland and Haroche) and might be judged as precision technology rather than a new physical effect, particularly before the second is actually redefined. There is also a real risk that I am letting the ease of attribution decide the ranking. I know that a clean attribution is not scientific merit. The Higgs discovery is the larger discovery by almost any measure, and by moving it down I may be choosing the comfortable prize over the important one. If the committee can find a defensible way to credit the Higgs experiments, that case remains stronger on pure importance. Ye's possible later relevance to the nuclear-clock candidate could also complicate a joint award, though it does not touch this prize.

responses.point: Olsson ranked the Higgs experiments sixth because the three names are founding spokespersons and proposers rather than those who made the decisive measurement, and the three-person limit fits a collaboration discovery poorly. She puts magic-angle graphene first.
responses.response: I accept her attribution objection against my own opening ballot. I argued that spokespersons and detector proponents were a defensible trio, but she is right that this is a judgement about leadership and not about who made the 2012 measurement, and I could not defend it line by line before the full committee. That is why I no longer put B053 first, although I still consider the discovery itself overdue. Where I disagree is on twisted bilayer graphene as the lead. I share her view that the observations are real and replicated. But the pairing mechanism is open, her own ballot concedes the credited set omits other early experimental groups, and Eriksson and Mehlig both note that Cao, the first author, is missing. I would rather wait than fix a prize motivation on a field that is still moving.

responses.point: Kroll ranked optical lattice clocks first as a measurement that changed what can be measured: 1e-18 uncertainties, millimetre-scale redshifts, and a route to redefining the second, with clean two-person credit.
responses.response: I agree with the substance of his case and it is the main reason for my change. Where I want more care is his remark that the committee need not wait for the redefinition of the second. I agree it is not required, but our citation should rest on the observed physics, the 1e-18 accuracy and the tests of fundamental constants, and not on a metrological decision that has not happened. I also want to hold him to his own caveat on overlap with 2005 and 2012. We should be able to state in one sentence what is new beyond the frequency comb and ion clocks, namely trapping many neutral atoms at the magic wavelength so that statistics and accuracy improve together.

responses.point: Pearce, our Chair, ranked IceCube first as a new observational window with a robust diffuse flux, and ranked the Higgs experiments second, stressing that attribution inside a collaboration is the main obstacle.
responses.response: I agree with him on the Higgs attribution problem and it is the reason I have moved. On IceCube I part company in degree only. The diffuse flux is secure, but the source picture is thin (a few objects, most of the flux unexplained), and Olsson's concern that earlier pioneers from DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA are not credited is not small. I put it second in my opening and keep it as an alternative, because it is real data about the cosmos and has the 2002 precedent. I would not give it priority over a precision result that is already independently reproduced in many laboratories.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked topological insulators first and treated magic-angle graphene as compelling but with a real attribution question, since the experimental first author and other groups are not in the credited names.
responses.response: I am sympathetic to his reasoning on graphene and it is part of why I am cautious there. I do not weigh topological insulators as heavily as he does, mainly because the 2016 prize already covered topological phases, and because he himself reports the 2D and 3D discoveries are partly separate and the credit is not cleanly split. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are not in the credited set and Zhang has died. I would need to see how the committee would write a citation that does not leave the HgTe prediction out before I could support a Kane, Mele and Molenkamp trio.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked clocks first on the grounds of precision understanding of atoms, while flagging that the overlap with Hall's and Wineland's earlier prizes means the committee has to show the new content is distinct, and that she has not verified the magic-wavelength attribution because other groups discussed the idea in parallel.
responses.response: This is the right caveat and I think it needs to be resolved before the final ballot. My reading is that Katori's proposal and first demonstration are the identifiable origin of the lattice scheme, and I would like the committee to say so explicitly, and to ask whether the parallel discussions she mentions (for example Pottier and Lemonde) predate his work in a way that affects the citation. I would not let it change the pairing, since nobody on the committee proposed a different pair, but I agree it should be checked and not assumed.

uncertainties: Whether the parallel magic-wavelength proposals by other groups affect Katori's priority and so the exact wording of the citation.
Whether the committee regards optical lattice clocks as a distinct discovery or as a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Whether a fair, rule-compliant three-person credit for the ATLAS and CMS Higgs discovery exists, which determines whether B053 should have been first all along.
My assessment of ATLAS, CMS and IceCube leadership roles comes from background knowledge and has not been verified against the committee record.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for any shortlisted candidate. My mentors and co-authors (Gross, Rubinstein, Van Riet) work in string theory and are not connected to any shortlisted ballot. I am Secretary and have commissioned reports as part of the procedure, but that is a role and not a personal connection to any candidate.
